newsitem.title: USA: China preparing market access offer-vice trade min.
newsitem.headline: China preparing market access offer-vice trade min.

text.p: Beijing is preparing to make a "serious" offer on opening markets to trading partners to help China's bid to join the World Trade Organization, Vice Minister of Trade Long Yongtu said Thursday.
"We are prepared to make a serious offer," Long said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
He said China will try to address the concerns of all of its trading partners. But he said that expectations should not get too high, otherwise they could be disappointed.
"I always tell them they have to be realistic," he said.
"China's WTO accession is only the beginning of market opening, it is not the end of it," he said.
U.S. officials have said Beijing needs to make a serious market access offer before China can be accepted into the global trading system.

Long said the latest offer would include proposals to provide more access for agricultural products and address some U.S. concerns about China's food safety rules, which Washington says are market barriers in disguise.

Long told Reuters the hope was that some kind of framework of an agreement between Washington and Beijing addressing the bilateral issues on China's WTO entry could be ready in time for the summit between President Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin later this year.
"Of course we would like to see this," Long said after the RFTV interview. "However, I do not know if it is possible."
Long, who is meeting with members of Congress during his visit, is expected to discuss WTO issues when he meets U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky next week.

Congress is getting ready to vote on President Clinton's decision to renew China's Most Favored Nation trade status for another year. The House Ways and Means Committee is expected to vote on a resolution to revoke China's MFN status later this month.

A committee aide said the panel, whose members for the most part support continued normal trade relations with China, is expected to agree to send the anti-MFN measure to the full House with a recommendation that their fellow lawmakers vote against it.

Groups of conservative and liberal lawmakers concerned about human rights abuses and nuclear proliferation issues are pushing to end China's MFN status, which allows Chinese goods into the United States at the same low tariffs on goods from most other countries.
Long told Reuters Financial Television that he would be surprised if MFN is revoked and that such a move would have a "very, very serious" impact on the entire relationship between the two countries.
"I am quite optimistic about the vote," Long said. "Because the Most Favored Nation treatment is in the best interest of both sides."
He said China hoped the United States would end the annual debate on trade relations because permanent MFN would put commercial relations on a more stable basis.
"I hope the relationship can improve because we firmly believe a good Sino-U.S. relationship is extremely important," he said.
